summary: Fire Atlas turns NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into an interactive burning-activity calendar. These satellites detect hot spots differently, so simply joining their records creates a misleading jump at the 2012 sensor change. Fire Atlas counts active map-cell days and uses years when both sensors operated to place earlier MODIS observations on a comparable VIIRS-scale record. Users can select an area, explore daily and monthly patterns, compare a period with the same dates in previous years, and identify unusually active months. The comparable historical record spans 2003 through 28 October 2026; recent raw detections appear separately. This gives responders, land managers, and scientists a clearer way to examine where and when detectable burning has occurred. Fire Atlas supports monitoring and research; it does not forecast fires or replace emergency alerts.
details:
Fire Atlas: Project Details

The problem: a new sensor can look like a sudden fire surge


Satellite hot spots reveal where intense burning was detected, including wildfires and agricultural burns. NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments have observed this activity for more than two decades, but VIIRS can detect smaller hot spots. Simply joining their raw records creates an apparent 2.64× jump around the 2012 handover. That jump alone cannot tell us whether burning changed or the instrument did.

Figure 1 : Global active cell-days, average 2013–2015 divided by average 2009–2011. Values are rounded for display.

Source: [Fire Atlas validation report].This is an internal continuity check, not proof of the true pre-2012 fire level.

Our solution: one comparable burning-activity calendar

Fire Atlas is a public web application that aligns the historical MODIS and VIIRS records, then makes the result explorable by place and time. The Python pipeline filters NASA FIRMS detections, counts a 0.05° map cell as active once per UTC day, and compares the sensors in years when they both observed the same areas. It estimates a conversion by 2.5° place and calendar month and applies it to the older MODIS observations. Missing satellite observations are marked as no data, rather than interpreted as zero burning.

The comparable historical record runs from 2003 through 28 October 2026. The daily display includes some 2002 observations, but that partial early period is flagged as indicative and is excluded from normal baselines. Recent raw FIRMS detections appear in a separate map layer; they are not mixed into the aligned historical series.

What a user does

1. Choose a place : Search for a country, use a preset, or draw an area on the map. The selected area can be shared through its URL.

2. Read the daily calendar : Darker cells show more detected activity. The calendar makes recurring fire seasons and unusual days visible at a glance.

Figure 2 : Actual calendar from the Fire Atlas website. Days before 2012 are indicative; 2003 is the start of the comparable baseline.

3. Ask whether a period is unusual : Choose the latest month, the last 30 days, or your own dates. Fire Atlas compares the selected period with those same dates in earlier years, showing the historical median, rank, and year-by-year values.

Figure 3 : Actual period-comparison view from the Fire Atlas website. The pictured values are an example from the published site guide, not a live alert.


4. Inspect longer patterns and share evidence : Monthly totals, seasonal views, and maps show how detected burning varies through time. Users can download CSV data, save charts, copy a share link, or print a one-page brief.

Figure 4 : Actual monthly-total chart from the website. The pre-2012 range describes uncertainty in converting MODIS to the VIIRS scale; it does not cover every source of satellite error.

What the checks show and what they do not

The raw global record steps by 2.640× across the sensor transition. The aligned record steps by 0.972×, close to the 0.964× MODIS-only reference. Fire Atlas also publishes backward and leave-one-year-out comparisons, uncertainty notes, and known limitations. The 2012 continuity result is partly within the years used to fit the method, so it is a consistency check rather than an independent proof. The conversion assumes that the sensor relationship measured during overlap years also applies before VIIRS existed; that cannot be observed directly.

Hot spots are active map-cell days, not counts of individual fires. Clouds, smoke, and missed overpasses can hide burning. The website does not identify whether a detection is a wildfire or an agricultural burn, and it does not predict future fires or replace official emergency alerts.

Data, technology, and intended benefit

The fire record comes from [NASA FIRMS] MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m detections. [NASA POWER] weather appears as context and does not change fire-activity values. The data pipeline uses Python with pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, and Shapely. The static website uses React, MapLibre, and Vite and is published on GitHub Pages. The method, validation report, source code, and limitations are available in the [public repository].

Fire Atlas gives responders, land managers, and researchers a clearer way to examine where and when detectable burning has occurred, compare a current period with its local history, and investigate unusual conditions while keeping the change of satellite sensor visible.
